terms.gloss: a little basket: the basket taken to market
evidence: Plaut. Men. 219: sportulam cape atque argentum
terms.comment: The basket that Erotium hands her cook with the money when she sends him to market for lunch, and so the word for a shopping basket. Later the sportula was also the basket of food, and then the money, that a patron gave his clients each day (Lewis & Short). For a picnic basket see “picnic basket”.

terms.gloss: a larger plaited basket for carrying

phrases.english: Put the apples in the basket.

phrases.latin: Sportula jam plēna est; carrulum petāmus.
phrases.english: The basket’s full already; let’s get a trolley.

phrases.latin: sportulam cape atque argentum. eccōs trīs nummōs habēs. — Habeō. — Abī atque obsōnium adfer; tribus vidē quod sit satis: neque dēfīat neque supersit.
phrases.english: Take the basket and the money. Look, here are three coins for you. — Got them. — Off you go and bring back the food; see that there’s enough for three, neither too little nor too much.

phrases.latin: dum loquor, ecce redit sportā piscātor inānī
phrases.english: while I speak, look, the fisherman comes back with an empty basket

sources: Lewis & Short: sportula · Lewis & Short: sporta
